A PROVISIONAL edge runs in paper/shadow, fully allowed, as long as the records stay source-tagged so a paper result can never masquerade as live evidence. Option D — live capital tagged as paper — is exactly the masquerade the article forbids.

questions.prompt_roman: A drift test starts failing after a config edit. THE DATA: `config/risk_constitution.yaml` was changed but the prose RISK_CONSTITUTION.md was not; `tests/test_risk_constitution.py` now fails on the mismatch.

options.A: Revert the yaml and ignore the prose.
options.B: Delete the drift test.
options.C: Edit the test to pass — it is just a test.
options.D: A failing drift test means prose and machine-twin diverged — amend BOTH together in one commit; never fix the test.

questions.stockfish_explanation: The drift test is a tripwire, not an obstacle. Its whole job is to scream when the human-readable law and the machine-readable twin disagree — which is exactly what happened. The fix is to reconcile prose and yaml together in the same commit so the law stays single-sourced; you never 'fix' the test to make the alarm stop (C), because that just lets the constitution and its enforcement silently drift apart. Editing or deleting the tripwire (C/B) is how the conscience layer rots.

questions.prompt_roman: Two caps could both apply to a set of positions. THE DATA: three carry-pair trades, each risking 0.7% (all under the 0.75% per-trade cap), total carry heat 2.1%; a fourth carry trade at 0.7% would push heat to 2.8%, over the 2.5% carry-complex cap.

options.A: Deny/trim the fourth — the binding constraint is the aggregate carry-complex cap (2.5%), which 2.8% breaches, even though every individual trade satisfies the per-trade cap.
options.B: Open it — the two caps are independent and per-trade wins.
options.C: Open it and net the risk against an equity hedge.
options.D: Open the fourth — each trade is under 0.75%, so all is well.

questions.stockfish_explanation: Per-trade and aggregate caps are BOTH binding, and here it's the aggregate that bites. Every leg is a well-behaved 0.7% (under 0.75%), but Article 2 treats the carry pairs as one correlated bet, and 2.8% total heat breaks the 2.5% ceiling. Passing the per-trade check does not exempt you from the complex check — 'each trade is small' is the exact rationalization that lets four small correlated bets become one oversized one. You trim the fourth until total carry heat is at or under 2.5%.

questions.prompt_roman: The most basic cap question. THE DATA: a trader wants to risk 1.2% on their single best idea of the month; Article 1 caps per-trade risk at 0.75%.

options.A: 2.0% — match the daily-loss cap.
options.B: 1.2% — best ideas deserve more.
options.C: 0.75% — no single trade may risk more than the Article 1 per-trade cap, regardless of how good it looks.
options.D: 1.0% — a reasonable compromise.

questions.stockfish_explanation: The per-trade cap is 0.75% and it applies to every trade, including — especially — your favorite one. The trades you're most excited about are the ones most likely to tempt you past the line, which is why the line is absolute. Confidence in an idea is not a sizing input. 0.75% and no more.

questions.prompt_roman: The deep drawdown rung is hit. THE DATA: peak-to-trough drawdown 6.7%; Article 3 — 6.5% flatten every predictive-layer position; the 8% trailing prop halt sits just above.

options.A: Do nothing until exactly 8%.
options.B: Halve sizes — treat 6.7% like the first rung.
options.C: Flatten every predictive-layer position — 6.7% is past the 6.5% rung, the last line before the 8% trailing prop halt.
options.D: Halt new entries but keep existing positions.

questions.stockfish_explanation: 6.5% is the emergency rung — flatten the entire predictive book. It's deliberately placed 1.5% below the binding 8% trailing prop halt so it can actually fire and save the account before the external line kills it; the original draft put this breaker above 8%, where it was a decorative brake that could never engage. At 6.7% you're past it, so you flatten predictive positions now. Waiting for 8% (A) is trusting the very line the ladder exists to keep you away from.

questions.prompt_roman: The scribe records dimension 6. THE DATA: S(t) dimension 6 is `rate_diff_z` (the IRP rate-differential z-score); today the external rate feed is unavailable.

options.A: Default rate_diff_z to 0.0 — it is an optional external-data dimension that falls back to 0.0 when unavailable, without breaking S(t).
options.B: Guess a plausible value from yesterday.
options.C: Drop to a 7-dimension vector.
options.D: Abort the whole state vector — one missing dimension is fatal.

questions.stockfish_explanation: The state vector is locked at exactly 8 dimensions, but two of them — rate_diff_z and cot_z — are explicitly optional because they depend on external feeds. When the feed is down, they default to a clean 0.0 rather than crashing the build or silently fabricating a value (B). You never drop to 7 dims (C) — the schema is frozen and a test guards it. Missing REQUIRED fields raise loudly; missing OPTIONAL ones fall back to 0.0. That's honest handling of absent data.

questions.prompt_roman: A required dimension is missing from the record. THE DATA: build_state() is called on a record lacking `atr_pct` (a REQUIRED field, dimension 3); rate_diff_z is also absent (optional).

options.A: The whole build silently returns zeros.
options.B: atr_pct defaults to the last known value.
options.C: Both default to 0.0.
options.D: Missing atr_pct raises a KeyError (required, no silent mocking); the missing optional rate_diff_z defaults to 0.0.

questions.stockfish_explanation: The builder draws a hard line between required and optional. atr_pct is core to the position's state, so its absence raises a KeyError — no silent mocking, no made-up fallback, you fail loud and fix the data. rate_diff_z is external-dependent, so its absence quietly becomes 0.0. Treating a missing REQUIRED field as 0.0 (C/A) would be exactly the silent-mocking failure the system forbids — you'd be trading on a fabricated state and not know it.

questions.prompt_roman: A dev wants to insert a new feature into the middle of S(t). THE DATA: STATE_DIMS is a locked 8-tuple in a fixed order; a test asserts the order can never silently drift; persisted S(t) depends on the order.

options.A: Insert it in the middle — order does not matter.
options.B: Do not reorder — changing STATE_DIMS is a breaking schema change; any new dimension requires a version bump everywhere S(t) is persisted, not a silent insert.
options.C: Append it and skip the version bump.
options.D: Insert it and update only the training code.

questions.stockfish_explanation: The dimension order is a contract, not a convenience. Everything downstream — the gym, the value scorer, any persisted state — reads S(t) positionally, so inserting a feature in the middle silently reassigns the meaning of every later dimension and corrupts every stored vector. The rule is explicit: changing STATE_DIMS is a breaking schema change that must bump a version marker everywhere S(t) is persisted. A silent insert (A) or an un-versioned append (C) is the kind of undocumented change that becomes expensive research debt later.

questions.prompt_roman: Compute dimension 8. THE DATA: `drawdown_from_peak` for a LONG position; best price since entry 1.1050, current close 1.1010, entry 1.1000.

options.A: 0.0 — the trade is still in profit versus entry.
options.B: About +0.36% — drawdown_from_peak measures retracement from the BEST excursion (1.1050 -> 1.1010), not from entry, so it is positive even while the trade is green.
options.C: Negative, because price is above entry.
options.D: Undefined without the ATR.

questions.stockfish_explanation: drawdown_from_peak is about giving back GAINS, not about being underwater versus entry. For a long, it's (best_price - close) / best_price = (1.1050 - 1.1010)/1.1050 ~ 0.36%. The trade is still above its 1.1000 entry, but it has retraced from its 1.1050 peak — and that retracement is what this dimension captures. Anchoring it to entry (A/C) misses the point: the state vector wants to know how much of the run-up the position has surrendered, which matters for trailing/exit logic.

questions.prompt_roman: An ICT setup forms outside the sanctioned windows. THE DATA: entries are allowed only in high-probability kill zones (London 02:00-05:00, NY_Open 07:00-10:00, NY_PM 13:30-16:00 UTC); this setup triggers during the NY lunch consolidation (12:00-13:30 UTC).

options.A: Take it at double size to compensate for the timing.
options.B: Take it but only for USDJPY.
options.C: Take it — a good setup is a good setup at any time.
options.D: Skip it — NY lunch is a blocked consolidation window; ICT entries only fire inside the high-probability kill zones.

questions.stockfish_explanation: In ICT, timing isn't a soft preference — kill_zone carries real weight and NY lunch is explicitly a blocked, low-participation consolidation window. A setup that looks perfect but fires at the wrong time is the wrong setup; institutional flow isn't there to fuel it. This is regime-appropriateness at the intraday scale (Tenet 2): the pattern is only tradeable when it appears in the right session, not whenever it happens to print.

questions.prompt_roman: The ICT ATR-spike veto is tested. THE DATA: current bar ATR is 3.4x the recent average; the pipeline has a hard ATR-spike veto at 3.0x that must not be auto-mutated.

options.A: Veto the entry — a >3.0x ATR spike trips the hard veto; violent, disorderly bars are not tradeable setups.
options.B: Trade it at half size.
options.C: Lower the veto to 4.0x so the trade qualifies.
options.D: Trade it — high volatility means a big move.

questions.stockfish_explanation: A 3.4x ATR bar is chaos, not opportunity — spreads blow out, stops get run, and the orderly structure ICT relies on is gone. The pipeline vetoes anything above a 3.0x spike, and that veto is a hard invariant flagged not to auto-mutate. Loosening it to 4.0x just to let this trade through (C) is defeating a safety rail to satisfy a single setup — precisely what a hard invariant exists to stop. When the tape goes violent, you stand aside.

questions.prompt_roman: A trader wants to lever an ICT signal into the macro book. THE DATA: an ICT sweep fires long on USDJPY intraday; the ICT edge is unproven (permutation p=0.52); the trader wants to use it to justify a multi-day macro USDJPY position.

options.A: Use it only for the stop, not the entry.
options.B: Use it — a signal is a signal.
options.C: Do not — ICT is an unproven intraday reference layer; it cannot justify a multi-day macro position, and doing so also violates the horizon-isolation wall.
options.D: Use it if inverted.

questions.stockfish_explanation: Two independent reasons this fails. First, evidence: ICT's permutation p is 0.52 — it isn't a proven predictive edge at any horizon, so it can't be the reason for a multi-day bet. Second, isolation: an intraday ICT signal feeding a multi-day macro position is exactly the cross-horizon feature-sharing the doctrine bans. Even option A — 'just the stop' — is fine WITHIN the ICT trade (that's what ICT is for), but here we're talking about justifying a macro trade, which it may not do. Right layer, right horizon, or not at all.

questions.prompt_roman: The ICT score gate is proposed for loosening to fire more trades. THE DATA: ICT currently fills only ~2 trades / 90 days because most A-grade setups expire unfilled; a dev proposes lowering min_grade_to_execute from A to B to 'get more trades.'

options.A: Raise risk-per-trade to compensate for few fills.
options.B: Lower the grade to B — more trades means more edge.
options.C: Do not loosen the grade gate — the bottleneck is FILL RATE, not the score gate; ICT is unproven (p=0.52), so lowering the execution grade just adds unvalidated, lower-quality trades.
options.D: Lower it to C for maximum volume.

questions.stockfish_explanation: This is a diagnosis error dressed as an optimization. The reason ICT barely trades isn't that the grade gate is too strict — it's that A-grade setups expire unfilled (a fill-rate problem). Dropping the execution grade to B or C doesn't fix fills; it just floods the book with lower-quality, still-unproven (p=0.52) trades, which is adding complexity/volume on top of an edge you haven't validated (Tenet 4). Fix the actual bottleneck (fills), don't loosen a quality gate to paper over it. And juicing risk-per-trade (A) to compensate is the opposite of what a system with an unproven edge should do.

questions.prompt_roman: State what ICT is actually FOR in the stack. THE DATA: ICT pattern edge is unproven (p=0.52, fails BH); yet the ICT engine is retained and used.

options.A: It is a structure/reference layer — kill-zone timing and TP/SL placement — retained despite being unproven as a directional predictor.
options.B: It is deleted because it is unproven.
options.C: It feeds the Forex macro engine its direction.
options.D: It is the primary directional predictor for intraday trades.

questions.stockfish_explanation: Hold two facts together: ICT is not a proven directional edge (p=0.52), and it's still useful. What it's genuinely good at is structure — session timing (kill zones) and sensible take-profit/stop reference levels. So it's kept as a reference layer, not thrown away (B) and not promoted to a predictor (D) or leaked into the macro engine (C). Knowing the difference between 'unproven as prediction' and 'useless' is the whole point — it earns its keep for what it actually does, not for a claim it can't support.

questions.prompt_roman: A feature is proposed for promotion to LIVE. THE DATA: OOS IC 0.22 (> 0.15), positive marginal contribution in walk-forward, but it DEGRADES on the 6-month holdout window.

options.A: Promote at half weight.
options.B: Promote and re-check the holdout next quarter.
options.C: Promote — two of three gates pass.
options.D: Reject — all three promotion gates must pass; holdout degradation is disqualifying regardless of a strong IC.

questions.stockfish_explanation: Promotion is a three-gate AND, not a best-of-three. IC > 0.15 and positive marginal contribution are necessary, but the holdout gate — no degradation on the 6-month held-out window — is the one that catches overfitting, and it's failing. A feature that looks great in-sample and on IC but falls apart on untouched data is precisely the kind the holdout is designed to reject. Promoting anyway (C/A) or promising to check later (B) is how overfit features reach live capital. All three, or it doesn't ship.

questions.prompt_roman: A headline Sharpe looks too good. THE DATA: a strategy reports Sharpe 2.10, but it was UNCOSTED and annualised as if trading daily; the strategy actually trades 4-14 times per year. Properly costed and de-annualised, OOS Sharpe is ~1.08-1.25.

options.A: Report 2.10 — it is the raw computed number.
options.B: Report the costed, correctly-annualised ~1.08-1.25 — the 2.10 was inflated by ignoring costs and mis-annualising a low-frequency strategy as daily.
options.C: Report 2.10 but footnote the costs.
options.D: Average them to ~1.6.

questions.stockfish_explanation: A headline number built on two errors isn't conservative-or-aggressive, it's just wrong. The 2.10 ignored trading costs AND annualised a strategy that trades a handful of times a year as if it traded daily — both inflate the ratio. The honest figure is the costed, properly-de-annualised ~1.08-1.25. You don't footnote a wrong number (C) or split the difference (D); you report the correct one. Overstating your own edge is a form of self-deception that eventually gets paid for in live size.

questions.prompt_roman: A gate proposal is walked back after fresh data. THE DATA: HYP-044 proposed a VIX gate on the carry book; out-of-sample it was REJECTED (p=0.50, effect delta ~0); it has been rolled back. A new session re-proposes the same VIX gate because 'VIX obviously matters for carry.'

options.A: Re-add the VIX gate — VIX clearly matters for carry.
options.B: Do not re-add it — it was tested OOS and rejected (p=0.50, delta ~0); re-proposing it on intuition ignores recorded evidence and repeats buried work.
options.C: Re-add it at half strength.
options.D: Re-add it only in RISK_OFF.

questions.stockfish_explanation: 'VIX obviously matters for carry' is intuition — and this exact intuition was already tested and killed. HYP-044's VIX gate came back p=0.50 with essentially zero effect out-of-sample, and it was rolled back. Re-proposing it because it feels right is precisely the research-debt failure Tenet 6 guards against: the finding was recorded so nobody re-litigates it, yet here we are. Reviving a rejected hypothesis needs NEW evidence and the graveyard sign-off process, not a fresh appeal to intuition. The ledger already answered this.

questions.prompt_roman: Two edges are compared for how much to trust them. THE DATA: the forex macro edge has permutation p<0.001; the ICT pattern edge has permutation p=0.52 and fails Benjamini-Hochberg.

options.A: Trust ICT more — it trades more often.
options.B: Distrust both — p-values are meaningless.
options.C: Trust them equally — both are in production.
options.D: Trust the macro edge as proven (p<0.001) and treat ICT as unproven (p=0.52) — being in production does not make an edge statistically validated.

questions.stockfish_explanation: 'It's in production' and 'it's statistically proven' are different claims, and conflating them is the mistake. The macro edge clears the bar convincingly (p<0.001) — that's a real, validated signal. ICT sits at p=0.52 and fails multiple-comparison correction — a coin flip, unproven. Both can be in the stack (ICT as a reference layer), but you calibrate how much you TRUST each to its actual evidence. Trading frequency (A) has nothing to do with validity, and throwing out p-values entirely (B) discards the only honest scorekeeping you have.

questions.prompt_roman: A single walk-forward window looks damning. THE DATA: the forex macro edge printed -0.13 in the last range-bound year; a reviewer concludes the edge is fake and should be scrapped, ignoring the +0.51 / +1.26 trending years and the p<0.001 permutation test.

options.A: Do not scrap it — one negative range-bound year is consistent with a REAL but regime-fragile edge; the permutation test (p<0.001) and the trending-year returns show the edge is real and conditional.
options.B: Scrap it and rebuild from scratch.
options.C: Double its size to prove it works.
options.D: Scrap it — a negative year proves it is fake.

questions.stockfish_explanation: A single bad year in the WRONG regime doesn't falsify a regime-conditional edge — it confirms the condition. The macro edge is proven real (p<0.001) but only pays in rate-trending regimes; a -0.13 in a range-bound year is exactly what 'regime-fragile' predicts, sitting right next to +0.51 and +1.26 in trending years. Scrapping on one out-of-regime window (D/B) throws away a real edge because you judged it in the environment it was never meant to work in. The right response is regime-gating, not deletion — and definitely not doubling size (C).

questions.prompt_roman: A cross-AI session hands over a claimed result to be acted on. THE DATA: a prior session's notes claim a hypothesis was CONFIRMED and a rule already wired live; the hypothesis ID and the wiring cannot be found anywhere in the filesystem or ledger.

options.A: Delete the conflicting ledger to resolve the mismatch.
options.B: Act on it — the prior session confirmed it.
options.C: Verify against the filesystem/ledger first — a claimed confirmation with no findable prereg, ledger entry, or code is unverified and must not drive live action until reconciled.
options.D: Act on it and log it afterwards.

questions.stockfish_explanation: A confident claim from another session is a hypothesis about the repo, not ground truth — and here the evidence doesn't exist on disk. The discipline is to verify against the actual filesystem and ledger before anything touches live capital; a 'CONFIRMED' with no findable prereg, no ledger row, and no wired code is a phantom result, and acting on phantoms is how bad state propagates. You reconcile first, act second. Deleting the conflicting ledger (A) to make the mismatch go away is destroying the very evidence Tenet 6 says to protect.
